uncited: *   **Inputs:** A set of $P$ 3D Gaussians; a mini-batch of $B$ viewpoints (camera poses and intrinsics); tile resolution and screen dimensions.
*   **Outputs:** Rendered images for all $B$ viewpoints; gradients for Gaussian parameters (position, scale, rotation, opacity, color) propagated back from the loss function.
The core data structure is an array of projected Gaussian attributes.
*   16-bit viewpoint index (identifying which of the $B$ viewpoints the Gaussian belongs to)
For each of the $B$ viewpoints in the mini-batch, determine which of the $P$ total Gaussians are visible within the camera frustum.
Allocate memory only for the Gaussians identified in Step 1.
Let $N$ be the total number of Gaussian instances remaining after culling across all viewpoints.
Duplicate projected Gaussians for each tile they cover.
Assign each duplicated Gaussian a unique 64-bit ID using the multi-view format (16-bit tile, 16-bit viewpoint, 32-bit depth).
Sort the array of projected Gaussians by their 64-bit ID.
The rasterizer allocates multiple rendering blocks per tile—one block for each viewpoint.
*   **Number of Viewpoints ($B$):** The number of viewpoints rendered per mini-batch.
*   **Preprocessing Overhead:** While rendering overhead is mitigated, the preprocessing steps (culling, sorting, ID assignment) remain.
*   **Strengths:** Reduces gradient variance, improves convergence, and lowers memory usage compared to rendering all views independently.
*   **When to Use:** When training speed and convergence are prioritized, and hardware memory allows for multi-view processing.
It addresses the limitations of single-view training by leveraging multiple viewpoints per iteration to stabilize gradients.
The approach builds on the 3DGS rasterizer [2813-3d-gaussian-splatting-differentiable-rasterizer.md] and modifies its preprocessing and sorting stages to handle multi-view data efficiently.
